timeline.title: The Golden Age & The Outlaws
timeline.description: Before the 'electro' was even a thought, swing was the world's original version of punk rock. It was forged in the smoky, high-stakes atmosphere of Prohibition-era speakeasies—a time when music was an act of defiance. This era was defined by massive 16-piece orchestras, the virtuosic 'galloping' guitars of Gypsy Jazz, and a rhythmic soul so infectious it forced people onto the dance floor. These decades provided the raw DNA—the crackling vinyl vocals and triumphant brass stabs—that modern producers still hunt for in record crates today.

timeline.title: The Sampling Revolution
timeline.description: After spending decades gathering dust in attic collections, swing found a second life through the rise of digital sampling. In the 90s, a handful of experimental producers realized that the sophisticated swing of the 1930s possessed a strange, haunting chemistry when paired with the heavy sub-bass of modern hip-hop and house music. It wasn't quite a movement yet; it was a series of 'what-if' moments—lonely experiments in late-night studios that proved vintage elegance and futuristic grit belonged together.

timeline.title: The Austrian Blueprint
timeline.description: This is the moment the genre found its heartbeat and its name. Led by the pioneering sound of Parov Stelar, the movement moved out of the lounge and into the warehouse rave. By stripping away the complexity of traditional jazz and replacing it with a relentless 4/4 electronic pulse, the genre became a global phenomenon. It was an era of peak energy where tracks like 'We No Speak Americano' dominated the airwaves, and the subculture began to find its visual identity in a blend of vintage waistcoats, flat caps, and high-octane swing dancing.

timeline.title: Neon, Robots, and Bass
timeline.description: Today, electroswing has evolved into a total sonic chameleon, shedding its 'novelty' skin to become a sophisticated pillar of electronic music. It has splintered into wild new directions, merging with the aggressive bass of Dubstep, the rapid-fire breaks of Drum & Bass, and the cozy nostalgia of Lo-fi. It has also become a massive visual movement, defined by dark, surreal 'rubber-hose' animations and a steampunk aesthetic. It’s no longer just a tribute to the past; it’s a vision of a neon-lit future where the spirit of the Roaring Twenties never actually stopped.
